articles.title: NASA’s asteroid Bennu samples reveal a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
articles.summary: Tiny samples from asteroid Bennu are rewriting scientists' understanding of how our Solar System formed. New evidence suggests that Bennu was born where material from the inner and outer Solar System mixed, with Jupiter playing a surprising role in shaping its formation.
articles.content:
Samples collected from asteroid Bennu by NASA are revealing surprising new details about how our Solar System formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago. A new chemical analysis challenges earlier theories about the asteroid's birthplace and suggests that Jupiter played an important role in shaping the materials from which Bennu and other ancient objects formed.

Bennu completes one orbit around the Sun every 1.2 years and makes a relatively close approach to Earth about every six years, coming within roughly 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles). NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission traveled to the asteroid, collected material from its surface, and successfully delivered the samples to Earth in 2023.

On September 23, 2023, a capsule carrying approximately 120 grams of asteroid material landed in the Utah desert. Scientists around the world subsequently received small portions of the precious cargo for detailed study.

Among them was Maria Schönbächler, Professor of Isotope Geochemistry at ETH Zurich, whose laboratory received half a gram of Bennu material. Her team immediately began examining the samples for clues about the asteroid's history.

The research, now published in Science Advances, has uncovered a distinctive chemical signature that not only helps identify Bennu's origins but also provides new evidence about the processes that shaped the early Solar System.

Bennu's Chemical Fingerprint Reveals Its Cosmic Relatives

To investigate Bennu's origins, the ETH Zurich researchers examined isotopes of three elements: iron, titanium, and chromium.

Isotopes are different forms of the same chemical element that contain varying numbers of neutrons, giving them slightly different masses. By measuring the relative amounts of these isotopes, scientists can identify a material's chemical fingerprint. These patterns provide clues about where an asteroid's ingredients originated and, in some cases, when they formed.

The analysis revealed that iron and titanium are distributed remarkably evenly throughout Bennu's material. It also uncovered a close chemical relationship between Bennu, the asteroid Ryugu, and a rare group of primitive meteorites known as CI meteorites.

CI meteorites are carbon-rich remnants of the early Solar System that have undergone relatively little alteration over billions of years. They are exceptionally uncommon among meteorites recovered on Earth.

Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites share strikingly similar isotopic fingerprints, suggesting that their original materials came from the same reservoir of ancient cosmic dust. Their chemical signatures also differ substantially from those of other known asteroids, meteorite groups, and planets.

These similarities offer an important clue about where these objects formed and what conditions existed during the Solar System's earliest stages.

Scientists Discover Bennu's Unexpected Birthplace

For years, researchers generally believed that primitive asteroids like Bennu originated in the outer Solar System, perhaps in the same distant regions where comets formed. They also suspected that Bennu's original material came together relatively late in the Solar System's development.

The new findings challenge both assumptions.

Instead, the researchers propose that the material that became Bennu, Ryugu, and CI meteorites accumulated near a boundary known as the water-ice line.

This boundary marks the region in the disk surrounding the young Sun where temperatures were low enough for water vapor to freeze into ice. Around 4.5 billion years ago, it may have been a particularly important meeting place for material traveling from different parts of the developing Solar System.

Dust originating in both the inner and outer regions mixed near this boundary. Water ice helped the smallest particles stick together, allowing them to gradually accumulate into larger bodies.

"Bennu is a hybrid: the material does not clearly match either the inner or the outer Solar System," says Schönbächler.

Its unusual chemical composition suggests that Bennu formed from a combination of materials originating in both regions rather than from a single, isolated source.

Jupiter May Have Played a Crucial Role in Bennu's Formation

The researchers also developed a scenario explaining how this mixing could have occurred, with Jupiter emerging as a key player.

Jupiter began forming extraordinarily early in Solar System history, within approximately one million years of the Sun's birth. At that time, the young Sun was surrounded by a rotating disk of gas, dust, and ice.

Within this disk, countless small particles gradually collided and stuck together, building larger objects through a process called accretion. Over time, some of these growing bodies became asteroids and planets.

As Jupiter rapidly increased in mass, its immense gravitational influence began reshaping the distribution of material throughout the disk.

The researchers suggest that the growing gas giant acted somewhat like a structural barrier, preventing most larger particles from crossing its orbital region while still allowing finer dust to move around it.

This fine material, originating from different parts of the disk, could then mix extensively near the water-ice line.

According to the proposed scenario, the parent bodies of Bennu and Ryugu, along with the objects that produced CI meteorites, formed from this thoroughly mixed material.

Jupiter may therefore have helped determine not only where these ancient asteroids formed but also which ingredients became incorporated into them.

Ancient Dust and Ice Reveal the Ingredients That Built Earth

The proposed formation scenario could also explain two of Bennu's most intriguing characteristics: its abundance of water-bearing material and its chemical resemblance to the Sun.

Near the water-ice boundary, ice could evaporate as temperatures changed, releasing water vapor that later condensed again in cooler regions. This process would have helped concentrate water in the material from which Bennu formed.

Meanwhile, Jupiter's influence may have limited the movement of larger particles, leaving the asteroid's parent material dominated by fine dust.

Because these tiny particles could circulate and mix efficiently throughout the disk, they preserved a chemical composition that closely resembles the overall elemental mixture found in the Sun.

The process is somewhat similar to the way fine household dust spreads and settles across many different surfaces rather than remaining in one location.

This extensive mixing could explain why Bennu's material retains such a representative sample of the ingredients present during the Solar System's earliest history.

"Bennu may offer our best glimpse of the original mix of chemical elements from which the terrestrial planets were ultimately built," as Schönbächler states.

Bennu is considered an exceptionally primitive asteroid because its material formed approximately 4.5 billion years ago and has experienced relatively little chemical alteration since then.

That makes its samples particularly valuable for reconstructing the conditions that existed before Earth and the other rocky planets finished forming.

By studying the asteroid's chemistry, scientists can better understand how the Solar System developed and which processes determined the composition of its planets.

Bennu's water-bearing minerals and organic compounds also make it important for investigating how early Earth obtained some of the chemical ingredients necessary for life.

Although these findings do not establish exactly how those materials reached our planet, they provide valuable evidence about where such ingredients originated and how they were distributed throughout the young Solar System.

A New Mission to Mars' Moon Could Reveal More

Despite the new discoveries, several questions remain unanswered.

"We are now wondering whether other asteroids have the same isotopic signature as Bennu and Ryugu," Schönbächler goes on to state.

Researchers also want to determine more precisely how Jupiter influenced the movement of dust and whether its gravitational effects were responsible for favoring the accumulation of particularly fine particles.

Additional asteroid samples could help scientists test the proposed formation scenario and establish whether Bennu's chemical signature is shared by other ancient bodies.

With the Bennu analysis now complete, Schönbächler is looking ahead to another opportunity to examine material from the early Solar System.

Japan's space agency, JAXA, is preparing a sample-return mission to Phobos, one of Mars' two moons. The mission is scheduled to launch at the end of October 2026, with the goal of collecting material from the Martian moon and bringing it back to Earth.

"It would be exciting to also obtain this material to analyse it in my laboratory," she says.

Schönbächler plans to apply to JAXA for access to the samples. However, the scientific community will need to be patient. The capsule carrying material from Phobos is not expected to return to Earth until 2031.

Those future samples could provide another important piece of the puzzle, helping researchers determine how different regions of the early Solar System exchanged material and ultimately produced the planets, moons, and asteroids we observe today.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific breakthrough from NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission, revealing new insights into the formation of the Solar System through analysis of asteroid Bennu's samples. This discovery has broad implications for understanding planetary formation, the distribution of water and organic materials essential for life, and Jupiter's role in shaping early Solar System materials. The story is focused, detailed, and presents a meaningful advancement in space science with potential long-term benefits for humanity's knowledge of our cosmic origins.
articles.personality_title: NASA samples from asteroid Bennu reveal new clues about Solar System’s birth
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Scientists have long studied asteroids to learn about how the Solar System formed over 4.5 billion years ago. Asteroid Bennu, visited by NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission, carries ancient material that can help answer questions about the early days of our cosmic neighborhood.

**What happened** – In 2023, NASA’s OSIRIS-REx mission returned about 120 grams of rock and dust from Bennu to Earth. Researchers, including a team at ETH Zurich, analyzed tiny samples and found a unique chemical fingerprint. This fingerprint shows Bennu’s material is a mix from both the inner and outer parts of the early Solar System. The study published in Science Advances also suggests Jupiter’s gravity helped shape this mix.

**Impact** – This discovery changes previous ideas that Bennu formed only far from the Sun. Instead, it formed near the “water-ice line,” a boundary where water vapor turned to ice, allowing dust from different regions to combine. Jupiter acted as a barrier, letting fine dust mix but blocking larger particles. Bennu’s composition closely matches rare meteorites and offers a snapshot of the original dust that built Earth and other planets.

**What’s next step** – Scientists want to see if other asteroids share Bennu’s chemical signature. They will also study how Jupiter’s gravity influenced the early Solar System’s dust. Meanwhile, Japan plans to send a mission to Mars’ moon Phobos to collect samples, expected back in 2031. These new samples could give more clues about how materials moved and mixed in space long ago.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Bennu samples show that early Solar System materials mixed near the water-ice boundary with Jupiter shaping this blend, offering fresh insight into how planets like Earth formed.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les échantillons de l’astéroïde Bennu de la NASA révèlent de nouveaux indices sur la naissance du Système solaire
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les scientifiques étudient depuis longtemps les astéroïdes pour comprendre comment le Système solaire s’est formé il y a plus de 4,5 milliards d’années. L’astéroïde Bennu, visité par la mission OSIRIS-REx de la NASA, contient des matériaux anciens qui peuvent aider à répondre aux questions sur les débuts de notre environnement cosmique.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2023, la mission OSIRIS-REx de la NASA a ramené sur Terre environ 120 grammes de roches et poussières de Bennu. Des chercheurs, dont une équipe de l’ETH Zurich, ont analysé de minuscules échantillons et découvert une empreinte chimique unique. Cette empreinte montre que le matériau de Bennu est un mélange provenant à la fois des parties interne et externe du jeune Système solaire. L’étude publiée dans Science Advances suggère aussi que la gravité de Jupiter a aidé à former ce mélange.

**Impact** – Cette découverte change les idées précédentes selon lesquelles Bennu s’était formé loin du Soleil. En réalité, il s’est formé près de la « ligne de glace d’eau », une limite où la vapeur d’eau se transformait en glace, permettant à la poussière de différentes régions de se mélanger. Jupiter a agi comme une barrière, laissant passer la poussière fine mais bloquant les plus gros grains. La composition de Bennu ressemble beaucoup à celle de météorites rares et offre un aperçu de la poussière originelle qui a construit la Terre et les autres planètes.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques veulent savoir si d’autres astéroïdes ont la même signature chimique que Bennu. Ils étudieront aussi comment la gravité de Jupiter a influencé la poussière du jeune Système solaire. Par ailleurs, le Japon prévoit une mission vers Phobos, une lune de Mars, pour ramener des échantillons attendus en 2031. Ces nouveaux matériaux pourraient apporter d’autres indices sur la façon dont les matériaux se sont déplacés et mélangés dans l’espace.

**Message clé en une phrase** – Les échantillons de Bennu montrent que les matériaux du jeune Système solaire se sont mélangés près de la limite de glace d’eau, Jupiter jouant un rôle clé, offrant ainsi un nouvel éclairage sur la formation des planètes comme la Terre.
articles.personality_title_es: Las muestras del asteroide Bennu de la NASA revelan nuevas pistas sobre el nacimiento del Sistema Solar
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los científicos han estudiado durante mucho tiempo los asteroides para entender cómo se formó el Sistema Solar hace más de 4.500 millones de años. El asteroide Bennu, visitado por la misión OSIRIS-REx de la NASA, contiene material antiguo que puede ayudar a responder preguntas sobre los primeros días de nuestro vecindario cósmico.

**Qué pasó** – En 2023, la misión OSIRIS-REx de la NASA trajo a la Tierra unos 120 gramos de roca y polvo de Bennu. Investigadores, incluyendo un equipo de ETH Zurich, analizaron pequeñas muestras y encontraron una huella química única. Esta huella muestra que el material de Bennu es una mezcla del interior y exterior del joven Sistema Solar. El estudio publicado en Science Advances también sugiere que la gravedad de Júpiter ayudó a formar esta mezcla.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento cambia las ideas anteriores que decían que Bennu se formó solo lejos del Sol. En cambio, se formó cerca de la “línea de hielo de agua”, un límite donde el vapor de agua se congelaba, permitiendo que el polvo de diferentes regiones se mezclara. Júpiter actuó como una barrera, dejando pasar polvo fino pero bloqueando partículas más grandes. La composición de Bennu es muy parecida a meteoritos raros y ofrece una imagen del polvo original que construyó la Tierra y otros planetas.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren saber si otros asteroides tienen la misma firma química que Bennu. También estudiarán cómo la gravedad de Júpiter influyó en el polvo del joven Sistema Solar. Mientras tanto, Japón planea enviar una misión a Fobos, la luna de Marte, para traer muestras que llegarán en 2031. Estas nuevas muestras podrían dar más pistas sobre cómo los materiales se movieron y mezclaron en el espacio hace mucho tiempo.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Las muestras de Bennu muestran que los materiales del joven Sistema Solar se mezclaron cerca de la línea de hielo de agua, con Júpiter jugando un papel clave, dando una nueva visión sobre cómo se formaron planetas como la Tierra.

articles.title: Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
articles.summary: The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.
articles.content:
Scientists have uncovered a surprisingly complex network of magnetic structures hidden above regions of the Sun that appear relatively calm. Using the Sunrise-III solar observatory, which traveled high into Earth's stratosphere aboard a balloon in 2024, an international research team led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan (NAOJ) discovered intricate, thread-like magnetic features that had previously been difficult to observe.

The findings reveal that even the Sun's seemingly quiet regions contain elaborate magnetic structures. They also offer new clues to how energy travels upward through the solar atmosphere and contributes to its heating.

A Hidden Web of Magnetic Threads Above the Sun

Sunrise-III detected numerous thin, elongated magnetic structures woven into a larger network of magnetic fields above a quiet region of the Sun. This network, known as the magnetic canopy, extends through the chromosphere, a layer of the solar atmosphere located above the Sun's visible surface.

The canopy develops as magnetic fields concentrated at the solar surface (photosphere) spread outward and arch upward into the chromosphere (chromosphere). Rather than forming a relatively smooth, uniformly expanding structure, however, the new observations reveal that the canopy contains many narrow, thread-like features.

To investigate how these structures form, researchers used computer simulations that successfully reproduced the patterns recorded by Sunrise-III. The results suggest that movements on the solar surface twist magnetic field lines, creating the intricate structures observed higher in the atmosphere.

The observatory also examined another quiet region near the solar limb (visible edge of the Sun). There, it measured magnetic fields within spicules, narrow jets of solar material that extend upward from the surface. These observations revealed how the distribution of magnetic fields changes with increasing height above the Sun's visible edge.

Why the Sun's Quiet Regions Are Difficult to Study

Although the Sun is constantly active, much of its surface lacks prominent features such as sunspots. Scientists describe these comparatively inactive areas as "quiet." They cover most of the Sun, making them especially important for understanding how our star behaves.

However, quiet does not mean magnetically inactive. These regions contain magnetic fields that are generally weaker than those found in more active areas of the Sun. Their subtle structures are difficult to measure, especially with telescopes on the ground, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere can blur fine details.

Sunrise-III was designed to overcome this obstacle by carrying a powerful solar telescope far above most of the atmosphere.

A Balloon-Borne Telescope Reveals New Solar Details

Sunrise-III is an international research project built around a 1-meter telescope carried by a high-altitude balloon. During its 2024 mission, the observatory floated approximately 35 kilometers (about 22 miles) above Earth in the stratosphere, where atmospheric interference is greatly reduced.

This elevated vantage point allowed the telescope to capture exceptionally detailed measurements of the Sun's magnetic fields.

The balloon's gondola carried three scientific instruments developed through contributions from different countries. One of these was SCIP (Sunrise Chromospheric Infrared spectroPolarimeter), a near-infrared instrument developed under NAOJ's leadership.

SCIP is designed to measure magnetic fields continuously across different layers of the solar atmosphere, from the photosphere to the chromosphere. This capability allowed researchers to examine how magnetic structures extend and change with altitude rather than studying only a single layer.

New Clues to How the Sun's Atmosphere Is Heated

By observing from the stratosphere, Sunrise-III provided researchers with an unusually detailed picture of magnetic fields above the Sun's quiet regions. Its measurements revealed that the chromosphere contains far more intricate magnetic structures than a simple expanding canopy would suggest.

Understanding these structures could help scientists investigate how energy generated by motions near the solar surface is transferred into higher layers of the atmosphere.

The discovery offers an important step toward explaining how magnetic activity contributes to heating the Sun's atmosphere, including in regions that appear calm when viewed from afar.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about the Sun's magnetic structures using advanced balloon-borne technology, providing new insights into solar atmospheric heating. This breakthrough has broad implications for understanding solar physics, which affects space weather and Earth's environment, thus benefiting society at large. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights a meaningful advancement in space science.
articles.personality_title: Scientists discover hidden magnetic threads above the Sun’s quiet regions
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The Sun looks peaceful in many places, but those quiet areas hide complex magnetic activity. Studying these regions is hard because Earth’s atmosphere blurs telescope images.

**What happened** – In 2024, scientists used a telescope carried by a high-altitude balloon called Sunrise-III to study the Sun from 35 kilometers above Earth. They found thin, thread-like magnetic structures woven into a larger magnetic network above the Sun’s surface. These threads appear because twisting motions on the Sun’s surface shape the magnetic fields. The team also mapped magnetic fields inside narrow jets of solar material called spicules, showing how these fields change with height.

**Impact** – This discovery reveals that even quiet parts of the Sun have intricate magnetic structures. Understanding these threads helps explain how energy moves upward through the Sun’s atmosphere and heats it. Since the Sun’s magnetic activity affects space weather and Earth’s environment, learning more about these hidden fields is important for science and technology.

**What's next step** – Researchers will continue using advanced instruments like Sunrise-III to study the Sun’s magnetic fields in more detail. These studies will improve models of solar activity and might help predict changes in space weather that can affect satellites and power systems on Earth.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Using a balloon-borne telescope, scientists uncovered delicate magnetic threads in the Sun’s quiet regions, offering new insights into solar energy flow and atmospheric heating.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des scientifiques découvrent des fils magnétiques cachés au-dessus des régions calmes du Soleil
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le Soleil semble calme dans certaines zones, mais ces régions cachent une activité magnétique complexe. Étudier ces zones est difficile car l’atmosphère terrestre brouille les images des télescopes.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – En 2024, des scientifiques ont utilisé un télescope porté par un ballon à haute altitude appelé Sunrise-III pour observer le Soleil depuis 35 kilomètres au-dessus de la Terre. Ils ont découvert de fins fils magnétiques tissés dans un réseau magnétique plus large au-dessus de la surface du Soleil. Ces fils se forment à cause des mouvements de torsion à la surface du Soleil qui façonnent les champs magnétiques. L’équipe a aussi cartographié les champs magnétiques à l’intérieur de jets étroits de matière solaire, appelés spicules, montrant comment ces champs changent avec la hauteur.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que même les parties calmes du Soleil possèdent des structures magnétiques complexes. Comprendre ces fils aide à expliquer comment l’énergie monte dans l’atmosphère solaire et la chauffe. Comme l’activité magnétique du Soleil influence la météo spatiale et l’environnement terrestre, mieux comprendre ces champs cachés est important pour la science et la technologie.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs continueront d’utiliser des instruments avancés comme Sunrise-III pour étudier plus en détail les champs magnétiques du Soleil. Ces études amélioreront les modèles d’activité solaire et pourraient aider à prévoir les changements de la météo spatiale qui peuvent affecter les satellites et les réseaux électriques sur Terre.

**Phrase clé** – Grâce à un télescope porté par un ballon, des scientifiques ont découvert de fins fils magnétiques dans les régions calmes du Soleil, apportant de nouvelles connaissances sur le transfert d’énergie et le chauffage de son atmosphère.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos descubren hilos magnéticos ocultos sobre las regiones tranquilas del Sol
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El Sol parece tranquilo en muchas zonas, pero esas áreas esconden una actividad magnética compleja. Estudiar estas regiones es difícil porque la atmósfera de la Tierra borra las imágenes de los telescopios.

**Qué pasó** – En 2024, científicos usaron un telescopio llevado por un globo a gran altura llamado Sunrise-III para observar el Sol desde 35 kilómetros sobre la Tierra. Encontraron finas estructuras magnéticas en forma de hilos, entretejidas en una red magnética más grande sobre la superficie solar. Estos hilos se forman porque los movimientos de torsión en la superficie del Sol moldean los campos magnéticos. El equipo también midió los campos magnéticos dentro de jets estrechos de material solar llamados espículas, mostrando cómo cambian con la altura.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento muestra que incluso las partes tranquilas del Sol tienen estructuras magnéticas complejas. Entender estos hilos ayuda a explicar cómo la energía sube a través de la atmósfera solar y la calienta. Dado que la actividad magnética del Sol afecta el clima espacial y el ambiente en la Tierra, conocer mejor estos campos ocultos es importante para la ciencia y la tecnología.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores seguirán usando instrumentos avanzados como Sunrise-III para estudiar más a fondo los campos magnéticos del Sol. Estos estudios mejorarán los modelos de actividad solar y podrían ayudar a predecir cambios en el clima espacial que afectan a satélites y sistemas eléctricos en la Tierra.

**Frase clave** – Usando un telescopio en un globo, científicos descubrieron delicados hilos magnéticos en las regiones tranquilas del Sol, ofreciendo nuevas ideas sobre el flujo de energía y el calentamiento de su atmósfera.
